extracted.intended_audience: students and educators (people learning how to read and analyze editorial/political cartoons)
extracted.subtask_description: A step-by-step guide for examining and interpreting editorial or political cartoons, focusing on identifying characters, symbols, setting, perspective, and rhetorical devices and supporting inferences with evidence. Intended to help learners and teachers systematically unpack meaning and point of view in visual political commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall observation (people, items, actions, words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Look at the cartoon and think about the people, items, actions portrayed, and words within the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with an open, careful viewing: note everything visible — figures, objects, gestures, labels, speech or caption text — before interpreting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify who is in the cartoon
rubrics_metrics.description: Who is in the cartoon? Can you identify specific people? How do you know who the people are? If you can't identify specific people by name, who might the people portrayed represent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use visual cues (labels, caricatured features, clothing, context) and textual cues to determine identities; when names aren't clear, infer groups, roles, or archetypes the figures represent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view / whose story is told
rubrics_metrics.description: Whose story is being told? How would the cartoon change if it were told from a different point of view?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider narrator/subject perspective and how framing, emphasis, or omission shapes the narrative; imagine alternative perspectives to test bias or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spatial breakdown (quadrant analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Break the cartoon into quadrants. What details do you see in each quadrant? Top left: Top right: Bottom left: Bottom right:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematically inspect different areas of the image to catch details you might miss with a single glance; record distinct elements or focal points in each quadrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objects and their importance
rubrics_metrics.description: What objects (tools, signs, vehicles, furniture, technology, etc.) are in the cartoon and why are the objects important?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List objects and consider literal function and symbolic or contextual meaning (e.g., a ballot box, a flag, a smartphone); ask how each object contributes to the cartoon's message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting: time and place
rubrics_metrics.description: What can you figure out about the setting (time--year or decade, place), and how do you know? Why is the setting important?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use clothing, technology, references, captions, or text to date and locate the scene; explain how setting influences interpretation or relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character information from actions, words, and reactions
rubrics_metrics.description: You learn about characters from what they do and say and how others react to them. What can you learn about the people in the cartoon from these things?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze gestures, expressions, dialogue, and interactions to infer motivations, relationships, and attitudes; cite specific behaviors as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Are any symbols used in the cartoon? What are they and what do they symbolize?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify conventional or context-specific symbols (e.g., eagle for nation, scales for justice) and explain their intended meaning within the cartoon's context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbols' importance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain how symbols condense complex ideas, signal values or associations, or steer the viewer toward particular interpretations; relate back to overall argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there any metaphors in the cartoon? What are they?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect visual or verbal metaphors (e.g., depicting an institution as a sinking ship) and explain the comparison being made and its rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: What information does the caption provide? Does it support the drawing or provide a different perspective?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare caption text to imagery: does it clarify, contradict, add irony, or reframe the visual message? Use this to refine interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferences supported by evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: What can you infer from this cartoon? List evidence to support your answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit interpretive claims (author's position, critique, or message) and pair each inference with concrete visual or textual evidence from the cartoon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's viewpoint / stance
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the viewpoint of the artist? How do you know (list evidence from the cartoon to support your answer)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the cartoonist's perspective (critical, supportive, satirical, neutral) and cite features — tone, caricature treatment, captions, symbols, emphasis — that reveal this stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Questions raised and follow-up sources
rubrics_metrics.description: What questions does the cartoon raise in your mind? Where might you find answers to those questions?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note informational gaps or contextual queries (who/what/when/how) and suggest research resources (news articles, background sources, archives, referenced people/events) to verify or deepen understanding.
